text:
Emma's six most common words are to, the, and, of, I and a. Not one of them says what the novel is about. Drop the stopwords and count again: Mister, Emma, could, would, Missus, Miss. Now the heroine's name comes second. Raw frequency rewards the commonplace. Filter first, and the topic comes through. But a count only sees spelling. It can't tell what job a word is doing.

Take fish. In I caught a big fish, it's a noun. In we fish on weekends, it's a verb. Same spelling, two jobs, and a counter can't tell them apart. Part-of-speech tagging labels every word with its job, judged from the words around it. NLTK's tagger learned from text that people tagged by hand. It calls the first fish NN, a noun, and the second VBP, a verb.

Those labels are Penn Treebank tags. The tall man reads books comes back as DT, JJ, NN, VBZ and NNS. A determiner, an adjective, a noun, a present-tense verb, and a plural noun. There are about thirty-six, but the first letter does most of the work: N for nouns, V for verbs, J for adjectives, R for adverbs. That's enough to pull patterns out of text. Tag the talented young engineer quietly designed a brilliant new system, and keep the tags that start with N. You get the nouns: engineer and system. J gives the adjectives, talented, young, brilliant and new. V gives designed, and R, quietly.

Tags fix lemmatizing, too. The WordNet lemmatizer treats every word as a noun, unless it's told otherwise. So in the runners were running and they had eaten well, running and eaten come back untouched. Tag first, hand each word its tag, and running becomes run, eaten becomes eat. Even were and had become be and have. Tag, then lemmatize: that's the accurate recipe. Still, every step so far looks at one word at a time.
